claims.text: Optimally homogenizing lattice strain in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts enhances ethanol-oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability relative to an unannealed baseline.
The as-synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst consists of 2–5 nm nanoparticles.
The unannealed PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has a heterogeneous lattice-strain distribution.
Changing annealing temperature can modulate lattice strain in PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles.
Thermal annealing makes the lattice-strain distribution of PtPdRhRuIrOs more uniform.
Post-annealing verification that particle size and composition are unchanged is sufficient to isolate lattice strain as the only modified variable.
XRD peak shifts and broadening can characterize the lattice-strain distribution.
High-resolution TEM strain mapping can measure the local lattice-strain distribution.
Atom probe tomography can correlate local strain with surface atomic configurations.
A more uniform strain distribution shifts the d-band centers of surface atoms in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
A shift in the surface d-band center changes adsorption and desorption energies of reactants and reaction intermediates.
Optimized adsorption of intermediates and poisoning species minimizes catalyst poisoning.
Strain-mediated electronic and adsorption changes enhance ethanol-oxidation kinetics and activity.
Reduced poisoning caused by optimized strain improves catalyst durability.
Optimized strain enhances selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Performance follows a volcano-shaped dependence on annealing temperature, with an optimum near 500°C.
The proposed strain–performance relationship holds for 2–5 nm particles in 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature during cycling from 0.1 to 1.0 V versus RHE.
A significant annealing-induced change in strain without the predicted volcano-type change in catalytic metrics would falsify the proposed strain-governed mechanism.
